opus-5.5.text:
I think the starting point is to look honestly at what rule-based RL has actually given us. Over the past year or so, the big wins have come from domains where you can write down a clean verifier: math problems with a definite answer, code that either passes the unit tests or doesn't, some games and puzzles. In those settings you set up the environment, you define the reward rule, and the model can improve itself through massive trial and error. That's real progress, and I don't want to downplay it.

But if you step back, the bottleneck is quite obvious. Every one of those successes depends on a human first designing the task, designing the environment, and designing the reward. The model is still learning inside a box that we built for it. And the space of things we care about in the real world mostly doesn't come with a clean verifier. How do you write a rule-based reward for "did this research direction turn out to be insightful," or "was this a good conversation with this particular user," or "did the agent handle this messy, long-horizon task well"? You either can't, or the rule you write gets hacked very quickly. So rule-based RL scales with human engineering effort, not with the model's own experience. That's fundamentally the same limitation we had with supervised learning, just moved one level up.

When I say autonomous learning, what I mean is a system that can keep learning from its own interaction with the world without a human hand-crafting each reward. That involves a few things. First, the model has to be able to generate or recognize its own learning signals: to judge whether it made progress, to notice when its prediction about the world was wrong, to form something like intrinsic goals. Second, it needs to learn continually. Right now we have a sharp separation between training and deployment: you train, you freeze, you ship. Humans don't work like that. We learn while we're doing things, and the experience of doing the task is itself the training data. Third, it needs to handle very long horizons, where feedback is sparse and delayed, and that's exactly where hand-designed rules break down.

There's also a more philosophical reason. If you look at how intelligence emerged in nature, nobody wrote reward rules for each skill. There were some very low-level drives, and then the organism, interacting with an open-ended environment, figured out an enormous amount on its own. I'm not saying we need to copy biology, but it suggests that the leverage comes from the system's ability to learn from open-ended experience, not from us enumerating tasks.

So for me it's less of a "nice to have" and more of a necessity. If we keep relying on rule-based RL, progress will be capped by how many good environments and verifiers humans can build, and the model will stay strong in the narrow, verifiable domains and remain brittle everywhere else. To get to something that genuinely keeps getting smarter in the real world, the learning loop has to become autonomous. Exactly how to do that, through better world models, self-evaluation, memory, or some combination, is still very much open, and honestly that's what makes it the most interesting problem right now.

r001.rationale: It says most real-world tasks lack a clean verifier and that hand-written rules can be hacked.

r002.rationale: It says the model should generate or recognize its own learning signals and judge whether it made progress.

r003.rationale: It identifies human-designed tasks, environments, and rewards as a bottleneck that limits scaling.

r004.rationale: It mentions very long horizons and delayed feedback, but does not frame indefinitely long context as necessary because real environments unfold as ongoing, dynamic sequences.

r005.rationale: It does not identify learning from natural-language or unstructured environmental feedback as a technical challenge.

r006.rationale: It mentions intrinsic goals, but does not describe intrinsic rewards driving parameter updates to adapt to the world.

r007.rationale: It describes continual learning from the system’s own interaction with the world, including learning while doing tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
When we look at what's actually driving progress right now, it's reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. Math, code, anything where you can write a rule that checks the answer. And that works beautifully, but it has a ceiling built into it. The ceiling is that someone has to write the rule. Every task you want the model to get better at, a human has to sit down and define what "correct" means, build the environment, construct the reward. That's a form of annotation. It's more scalable than labeling data point by point, but it's still annotation, and it still scales with human effort.

The problem is that the tasks we care most about don't come with a checker. Doing research, running a long project, making judgment calls where the feedback arrives weeks later and is ambiguous. You can't write a rule for those. So if we keep going down the current path, we get models that are superhuman at exam-style problems and still fundamentally dependent on us to tell them what good looks like everywhere else.

That's why I think autonomous learning is not an optional next step, it's the necessary one. A system has to be able to generate its own problems, judge its own outcomes, and extract signal from the world without a human pre-packaging the reward. Think about how people learn. Nobody hands us a verifier for most of what we do. We form expectations, we act, we get surprised, and the surprise itself is the training signal. The model needs that loop internally.

There's also a very practical reason. Pre-training is running out of high-quality data, and rule-based RL is running out of cheaply verifiable tasks. Both of the current scaling axes have a visible end. The only axis that doesn't obviously saturate is experience. If the model can keep interacting with environments, keep proposing hypotheses, keep checking itself, then the data generates itself and the curve continues.

I'm not saying rule-based RL is wrong. It's the right thing to do today, and it's teaching us a lot about what reasoning looks like when it's optimized. But I see it as scaffolding. The goal is a model that learns the way a scientist learns, where the supervision comes from reality rather than from us. That's the direction we have to go, and honestly I think it's where the next real jump comes from.

r001.rationale: It says many important tasks lack a checker and that humans must define what “correct” means, limiting rule-based RL.

r002.rationale: It says the system must generate its own problems and judge its own outcomes, with the model’s learning loop operating internally.

r003.rationale: It identifies building environments and constructing rewards as human work that still scales with human effort.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss long context or the need to model real environments as ongoing dynamic sequences.

r005.rationale: It does not identify natural-language or unstructured environmental feedback as a technical challenge.

r006.rationale: It does not describe intrinsic rewards driving the model to update its parameters to adapt to the world.

r007.rationale: It describes continued learning through interaction with environments, including proposing hypotheses and checking outcomes.

astra-6.text:
I think the key issue is who defines what the system should learn. In rule-based reinforcement learning, we usually specify the task, the reward, and the conditions for success. The system can become very good within that setup, but those choices still come from us.

In an open environment, you cannot anticipate every situation or write a reliable reward for everything that matters. The system needs to recognize what it doesn’t understand, decide what to explore, and use what it learns in new situations. That is why I see autonomous learning as a necessary direction.

It doesn’t mean abandoning reinforcement learning. It means moving beyond learning only within a task we have already defined, toward systems that can help determine what is worth learning next—while remaining guided by human goals and constraints.

r002.rationale: The response says the system should help determine what to learn next, but does not clearly state that its evaluation mechanism should originate within the learner.

r005.rationale: It does not discuss learning from natural-language or unstructured environmental feedback.

r006.rationale: It does not describe intrinsic rewards driving the model to update its own parameters.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key limitation is that, in rule-based reinforcement learning, people still define much of the problem in advance: what actions are available, what counts as success, and how rewards are assigned. The system can become very good within that setup, but when the environment changes or a new problem appears, it often needs people to redesign the rules or the reward.

Autonomous learning means giving the system more ability to learn from experience: to explore, identify what it doesn’t understand, and adapt its behavior without waiting for a new set of instructions. Reinforcement learning can still be part of that. The important step is moving beyond optimizing a fixed objective toward learning how to handle situations we haven’t anticipated.

Of course, that also raises a difficult question: how do we give a system room to learn while keeping its behavior reliable? So I see autonomous learning as a necessary direction, but one where adaptability and oversight have to develop together.
